title: Report on Studying Abroad at Johns Hopkins University
paragraphs: From March 2010, I was allowed to train for three months at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, in the United States.

Johns Hopkins is one of the leading hospitals in the country, competing with Harvard every year for the title of No. 1 hospital in the United States, and doctors such as the one who discovered p53 and laid the foundations of today's cancer field, and the one who edits UpToDate, walk around inside the hospital. It also has an established reputation in education and enjoys tremendous popularity, and excellent students gather there. In such a blessed environment, I trained in Pulmonary, Emergency Medicine and GI.

First, in Pulmonary, I belonged to the consult team, was given patients to take charge of, did the first touch, and presented to the attending, including the Assessment/Plan. As a matter of principle, even for a student, a patient who had once been consulted on was followed until discharge, and I was surprised at how high the standard demanded of students was. They emphasised EBM, and I was handed papers about the cases I was in charge of and the next day had a discussion of the treatment policy based on them. I felt the need for the skill of reading medical English texts quickly. In the time outside consults there were lectures on X-rays and CT, which were very educational. The differences from the diseases seen in Japan were also interesting: the consults at JHU were very interesting, such as infections in patients with underlying diseases such as Cystic Fibrosis and HIV, or ILD. Next I trained in Emergency Medicine. The clerkship was on a shift system, with 16 eight-hour shifts required (including 2 night shifts and 2 weekend shifts), with lectures and so on in between, and it was a very meaningful clerkship. At the start of each shift I attended a resident and did the first touch with patients. From the interview to suturing and urinary catheterisation, I was allowed to do many things in most cases. The gunshot case I had been hoping for as a case I could not see because I was suturing another patient at the time, but there were many conditions rare in Japan, such as stabbings and drug abuse, and I enjoyed it very much.

In the ED, on the last day there was a case presentation. It involved explaining my own case, citing a paper related to it. After each presentation, there was lively questioning and discussion among the students, and then the attending would say that this point was excellent and explain it. I was very surprised at how good the local students were at discussion and how high the attending's teaching ability was.

The last department was GI, where I spent two weeks each on the liver team and the consult team. My job was, when a new consult came, to take charge of the patient and present to the fellow and attending. Liver transplantation was always one of the treatment options, and when making an Assessment I was always told to evaluate whether there was a benefit to liver transplantation, and there were many assessment scores, which was very educational. GI is one of the fields in which Japan is advanced, and many people had been to Japan for academic meetings, and I was treated very well.

On my last day at Hopkins, through the introduction of Dr. 尾崎 of psychiatry, I had the opportunity to have lunch with Professor 澤 of Hopkins, and listening to a world-famous researcher was very stimulating. Also, through Dr. 澤's introduction, I was shown the schizophrenia ward. Not only the clerkship as described above, I also enjoyed my life there very much. Playing soccer with friends I made there, going out for drinks and going to watch Major League games, there was not a day that was not fulfilling.

On weekends, I took part in an Easter party at an attending's home, and I was treated to meals with Dr. 西崎 in Philadelphia and with Dr. 兼井 and Dr. 浅井 in New York. Dr. 浅井 further let me stay at his home afterwards and gave me a glimpse of the life of a New Yorker. It was a very valuable experience to hear at close range from Japanese doctors working in America, and I keenly felt how wonderful the Frontier network is.

There were encounters with many people, both in America and in Japan before departure, whom I would never have met if I had not studied abroad. Those encounters were the best thing, with the greatest influence on my life, from this study abroad. I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the many people who gave me this wonderful opportunity: Dr. 粕谷, 長縄-san, the administrative staff 西尾-san and 青木-san, the doctors who came to the pre-departure training, the seniors who held the pre-departure training and told me useful information, and my classmates who always kept stimulating me. Thank you very much indeed.
